passage:
The question of whether the anonymous 1592 pamphlet "Greene's Groatsworth" was in fact composed by Robert Greene or by his editor Henry Chettle has divided literary scholars for more than a century. The internal evidence has always been ambiguous. The pamphlet contains turns of phrase characteristic of Greene's earlier work — certain compound epithets, a taste for rhetorical triplets, an affection for moralizing addresses to a dying author's imagined readers — but it also contains idioms, spellings, and metrical patterns uncommon in any other text Greene is known to have written.

The most persuasive case for Greene's authorship rests not on a count of features but on a reading of the pamphlet's argumentative shape. Greene's late works share a recognizable posture: the penitent speaker confessing his excesses, gesturing at the younger writers who will inherit the stage, and insisting that his own example be read as a warning. The Groatsworth adopts that posture with a fidelity no ordinary imitator is likely to have achieved. Chettle, a competent but conventional editor, had no prior history of sustaining such a voice across an entire work; Greene had produced variants of it three times before.

Nothing in the documentary record rules out Chettle's involvement in the details — the correction of copy, the insertion of a transitional phrase, the updating of a reference to a living playwright. What the internal evidence does rule out, in my view, is the stronger claim that Chettle composed the pamphlet and merely attached Greene's name. The argumentative architecture is too continuous with Greene's acknowledged work, and too foreign to Chettle's, for that hypothesis to bear the weight of the idiomatic anomalies on which it has been made to rest.
comparativeBPassage:
Recent stylometric work on disputed Elizabethan pamphlets has moved the authorship question onto new ground. Where earlier investigators relied on a reader's sense of characteristic phrasing, current methods count features that authors do not consciously control — the relative frequencies of common function words, the distribution of sentence lengths, the ratio of certain contractions to their full forms — and compare these profiles against an author's undisputed corpus. Applied to "Greene's Groatsworth," the technique returns a mixed result. The pamphlet's function-word profile falls within the range established by Greene's late works, though near its margin; several of its sentence-level features fall outside that range and within the range of texts known to be by Henry Chettle.

A natural reading of this pattern is that the pamphlet is substantially Greene's but has been worked over by Chettle in ways that affect measurable surface features without disturbing the deeper frequencies. That reading is consistent with what the documentary record suggests about Chettle's editorial role. Greene died shortly before the pamphlet went to press; someone had to ready the copy, and Chettle is the likeliest candidate.

The stylometric evidence therefore does not settle the authorship question in the form it has traditionally been posed. It is compatible with Greene as sole author whose text was lightly revised, with Greene as principal author whose text was more heavily revised, and — at the outer limit of the measurements — with Chettle as author of substantial portions working from Greene's materials. What it rules out is any account that treats the pamphlet as wholly the work of either man, and any account that treats Greene's voice and Chettle's voice as so distinct that their commingling would be visible on the surface.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is central to both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whether a measurable difference exists between the common-function-word profiles of Robert Greene and Henry Chettle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether the argumentative structure of a late Elizabethan pamphlet is a more reliable guide to authorship than its surface vocabulary

choices.label: C
choices.text: To what extent "Greene's Groatsworth" can be attributed to Robert Greene rather than to his editor Henry Chettle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether stylometric methods have generally superseded traditional literary judgments about authorship

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether Henry Chettle possessed the literary skill to sustain a penitent authorial voice across an entire pamphlet

explanations.correct: Passage A argues that the strong Chettle-sole-author hypothesis fails and Chettle's role is limited to details; passage B argues the stylometric data is compatible with a range of distributions of the pamphlet between the two. Both are working the same question: how much of the Groatsworth is Greene's.
explanations.A: Only passage B takes up function-word profiles directly; passage A does not.
explanations.B: This is a methodological question each passage implicitly engages, but neither passage poses it as its central question.
explanations.D: Neither passage frames its argument around the general standing of stylometric methods.
explanations.E: Passage A raises this as one consideration among several; passage B does not address Chettle's literary skill at all.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A presents a conclusion that passage B refutes using quantitative evidence unavailable to passage A.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A and passage B reach compatible but not identical conclusions about the authorship question by appealing to evidence of different kinds, each of which admits of a different sense of what it is to write in an author's style.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A argues for Greene's sole authorship on literary grounds, and passage B provides stylometric confirmation of that conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A and passage B arrive at incompatible attributions of the pamphlet to its two candidate authors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage B criticizes passage A's methodology without offering an alternative account of the pamphlet's composition.

explanations.correct: A reaches a negative conclusion (the strong Chettle-sole-author hypothesis is ruled out) resting on argumentative architecture; B reaches a negative conclusion (the wholly-one-author view is ruled out) resting on frequency data. Both treat 'style' — A as argumentative posture, B as unconscious surface frequencies — and their positive conclusions are compatible rather than identical.
explanations.A: Passage B does not refute passage A; it is compatible with passage A's conclusion that Chettle did not compose the pamphlet alone.
explanations.C: Passage B does not confirm sole authorship; it explicitly says the data are also compatible with more extensive Chettle revision.
explanations.D: Their attributions are compatible, not incompatible.
explanations.E: Passage B offers its own positive account of what the stylometric evidence rules in and out.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over

choices.label: A
choices.text: whether Henry Chettle had some hand in readying "Greene's Groatsworth" for the press

choices.label: B
choices.text: whether the evidence concerning the pamphlet's authorship is ambiguous on its surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: whether the features an author does not consciously control are in principle more informative about authorship than the argumentative shape of the author's work

choices.label: D
choices.text: whether Robert Greene wrote any portion of the pamphlet

choices.label: E
choices.text: whether stylometric methods have produced reliable results on other disputed Elizabethan pamphlets

explanations.correct: Passage A rests its case on 'argumentative architecture' and treats idiomatic anomalies as weaker evidence. Passage B rests its case on features 'authors do not consciously control' and treats argumentative impressions as superseded. They tacitly disagree about which kind of feature is more probative.
explanations.A: Passage A explicitly allows Chettle's editorial involvement; passage B says the same. Agreement, not disagreement.
explanations.B: Both passages accept that the internal evidence is mixed on its surface.
explanations.D: Both authors accept that Greene wrote substantial portions.
explanations.E: Neither passage discusses stylometric performance on other pamphlets; there is no basis for disagreement.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is treated as evidence of authorship in passage B but not in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The use of compound epithets characteristic of Greene's earlier work

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pamphlet's affection for rhetorical triplets

choices.label: C
choices.text: The posture of a penitent speaker addressing his imagined readers

choices.label: D
choices.text: The relative frequencies of common function words across the pamphlet's text

choices.label: E
choices.text: The updating of a reference to a living playwright

explanations.correct: Function-word frequencies are a purely stylometric feature introduced by passage B as characteristic of the new methods, and are absent from passage A's catalog of evidence.
explanations.A: Compound epithets are passage A's evidence.
explanations.B: Rhetorical triplets are passage A's evidence.
explanations.C: The penitent posture is passage A's central piece of evidence.
explanations.E: The updated reference to a living playwright appears in passage A as something Chettle might have inserted; passage B does not mention it.

questions.questionStem: The passages most strongly support which one of the following claims about the "idiomatic anomalies" mentioned at the end of passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage B would regard them as decisive evidence that Henry Chettle composed the pamphlet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage B would regard them as compatible with substantial Chettle revision of a text principally composed by Greene.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The author of passage A takes them to establish that Chettle corrected the copy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both authors regard them as the most probative evidence bearing on the authorship question.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The author of passage A regards them as outweighing the pamphlet's argumentative architecture.

explanations.correct: Passage B's 'natural reading' is that Chettle worked over the text 'in ways that affect measurable surface features without disturbing the deeper frequencies.' Idiomatic anomalies are exactly surface features, and B treats them as consistent with heavy revision, not as proof of sole authorship.
explanations.A: Passage B rules out the view that the pamphlet is 'wholly the work of either man,' so the anomalies cannot be decisive evidence for Chettle.
explanations.C: Passage A cites the anomalies as the basis of the opposing Chettle-authorship argument, not as establishing mere copy correction.
explanations.D: Neither author treats them as the most probative evidence; passage A explicitly downgrades them, and passage B treats frequency data as more informative.
explanations.E: Passage A treats the anomalies as unable to 'bear the weight' Chettle-authorship advocates place on them; architecture outweighs the anomalies in A's account, not the reverse.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the case made in passage A for attributing principal authorship to Greene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An additional undisputed late work by Greene was discovered in which the penitent speaker posture was absent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Careful analysis showed that Henry Chettle had, in two other pamphlets of the early 1590s, successfully sustained a penitent authorial voice modeled on Greene's across an entire work.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stylometric analysis showed that the pamphlet's function-word profile fell at the center of Greene's range rather than near its margin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Documentary records showed that Chettle had edited several of Greene's earlier works without introducing stylistic changes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Literary historians agreed that the pamphlet contained a transitional phrase of the kind Chettle was known to insert into others' work.

explanations.correct: Passage A's central claim rests on the premise that 'Chettle … had no prior history of sustaining such a voice across an entire work.' (B) directly contradicts that premise, undermining A's reason for treating the penitent posture as diagnostic of Greene rather than Chettle.
explanations.A: Passage A describes the penitent posture as present in three of Greene's late works; a fourth without it would not undermine the claim that the posture is characteristic of him.
explanations.C: This strengthens rather than weakens Greene's attribution; it does not undermine passage A.
explanations.D: Passage A already concedes Chettle's editorial involvement without stylistic overhaul; this is neutral at worst, supportive at best.
explanations.E: Passage A already allows that Chettle may have inserted transitional phrases; acknowledging one does not undermine the stronger structural argument.

questions.questionStem: In passage B, the observation that the pamphlet's function-word profile "falls within the range established by Greene's late works, though near its margin" functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: establish that Greene was the pamphlet's sole author

choices.label: B
choices.text: reject the quantitative methods described earlier in the paragraph

choices.label: C
choices.text: set up the subsequent claim that the data are compatible with a range of distributions of the pamphlet between Greene and Chettle

choices.label: D
choices.text: dispute passage A's characterization of Greene's argumentative architecture

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that stylometric and literary methods always converge on the same answer

explanations.correct: The 'near its margin' qualifier is what licenses the paragraph's next move: that heavier Chettle revision remains consistent with the data. The sentence functions to set up the later spread of compatible scenarios.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly denies that the data establish sole authorship.
explanations.B: The passage endorses the methods it describes; it does not reject them.
explanations.D: Passage B does not engage passage A's argumentative-architecture claim at all.
explanations.E: The passage does not generalize about convergence of methods; the convergence here is partial.

passage:
Canadian courts have held for several decades that the oral histories of Indigenous communities must be admitted as evidence in cases involving land claims and treaty interpretation. The holding addressed a genuine difficulty. The documentary record on which ordinary common-law adjudication rests was assembled by colonial officials whose interests in a dispute over land were rarely impartial, and the exclusion of oral testimony would systematically privilege the version of events favored by those officials. Admitting oral histories is therefore not a concession to cultural sensitivity but a correction of an evidentiary distortion.

The correction, however, has been implemented unevenly. Courts that admit oral histories in principle have sometimes proceeded, in practice, to discount them against any documentary source that contradicts them, on the ground that written records are more easily verified. That treatment reinstates, in the weighting of evidence, the very asymmetry that admission was supposed to remedy. The genuine achievement of the cases is threatened by this practice, and the remedy requires judges to assess each oral source on its own evidentiary merits — the continuity of its transmission, the community's procedures for verifying it, the consistency of its content across independent lines of transmission — rather than against a default preference for written sources.

None of this requires courts to treat every oral history as accurate, or to abandon the ordinary adversarial tools of cross-examination and corroboration. It requires only that the tools be applied evenhandedly, and that the criteria used to weigh an oral source be criteria appropriate to oral sources rather than those developed to assess a different kind of record.
comparativeBPassage:
The Canadian jurisprudence on oral histories has been praised for its willingness to admit testimony that earlier courts would have excluded. That willingness is real, and it reflects a genuine shift in judicial attitude. The deeper question, less often addressed, is whether a court acting within the common-law adjudicative framework can do more than admit such testimony — whether it can receive it on its own terms.

An oral history transmitted within an Indigenous community typically functions not as a discrete recollection of a past event but as a structured discourse: the authority of the account depends on who is entitled to tell it, the ceremonial setting in which it is told, the relationship of the teller to the ancestors named in it, and the corrections the listening community is entitled to make. Stripped from that setting, excerpted into affidavits, and subjected to adversarial cross-examination on individual factual assertions, the testimony loses much of the structure that, within the community, gives it its standing.

A court that admits such testimony but then assesses it by criteria the testimony was not designed to satisfy has not, strictly speaking, excluded it; but it has processed it through a format that converts it into something the testifying community would not recognize as the source it provided. Genuine reception would involve a court's willingness to let the community's procedures for verifying and correcting an account enter into the court's own weighing of the testimony — a step Canadian jurisprudence has so far taken only tentatively, and without a settled account of what it would require.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately captures a point on which the authors of the two passages agree?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Canadian courts have not yet fully realized the aim behind their decision to admit Indigenous oral histories as evidence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The admission of oral histories should be subject to the same rules of cross-examination that govern documentary evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adversarial cross-examination is intrinsically unsuited to the evaluation of oral testimony of any kind.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Canadian courts should abandon the common-law adjudicative framework in land-claim cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The admission of oral histories has been adequately implemented in the cases decided so far.

explanations.correct: Passage A: courts 'have sometimes proceeded, in practice, to discount' oral histories, reinstating the asymmetry that admission was meant to remedy. Passage B: genuine reception 'has so far [been] taken only tentatively.' Both characterize the implementation as falling short of the announced aim.
explanations.B: Passage A endorses evenhanded application of cross-examination; passage B argues that cross-examination applied in the ordinary way converts the testimony into 'something the testifying community would not recognize.' Not an agreement.
explanations.C: Passage A does not reject adversarial tools in principle; it asks only that they be applied evenhandedly.
explanations.D: Passage A operates within the framework and seeks its evenhanded application; passage B raises doubts but does not call for abandonment.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The passages reach the same conclusion about the shortfall in current Canadian practice, but passage A locates the shortfall in the weighing of admitted evidence while passage B locates it in the format through which the evidence is received.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A argues that Canadian jurisprudence has fully realized its aims, and passage B argues that it has not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A defends the admission of oral histories, while passage B opposes their admission on procedural grounds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A proposes reforms that passage B argues would be counterproductive.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A and passage B disagree about whether oral histories should be admitted as evidence at all.

explanations.correct: Both agree the current state of play falls short. A's diagnosis: the shortfall is in weighting — oral sources are discounted against written ones. B's diagnosis: the shortfall is upstream, in how the testimony is formatted for legal consumption. Same verdict, different explanations.
explanations.B: Passage A does not claim the doctrine is fully realized; it explicitly says the 'genuine achievement … is threatened' by uneven implementation.
explanations.C: Passage B does not oppose admission; it raises a subtler question about whether admission alone is sufficient.
explanations.D: Passage B does not argue A's proposed reforms (evenhanded weighting) would be counterproductive.
explanations.E: Both accept that oral histories must be admitted.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over

choices.label: A
choices.text: whether the documentary record of colonial Canada reflects partial interests

choices.label: B
choices.text: whether ordinary adversarial cross-examination, applied evenhandedly to oral histories, is sufficient for genuine reception of that testimony by a court

choices.label: C
choices.text: whether Indigenous oral histories should be admitted into evidence in land-claim cases

choices.label: D
choices.text: whether courts have historically discounted Indigenous oral histories against written records

choices.label: E
choices.text: whether common-law adjudication relies heavily on a documentary record

explanations.correct: Passage A holds that the ordinary adversarial tools are adequate if applied evenhandedly and with oral-specific criteria. Passage B holds that even evenhanded cross-examination strips the testimony of the structural features that give it its standing, so mere admission is not genuine reception. The disagreement is about the sufficiency of evenhanded adversarial handling.
explanations.A: Both accept that the colonial record reflects partial interests (A explicitly, B implicitly via the 'shift in judicial attitude' framing).
explanations.C: Both accept that admission is appropriate.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the two passages taken together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The remedy passage A proposes — the evenhanded application of adversarial tools with oral-specific criteria — would resolve all of the concerns passage B raises about genuine reception of oral histories.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage B would regard passage A's proposed remedy as an improvement over current practice but as insufficient to achieve genuine reception of oral histories by the court.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both authors believe that the community's own procedures for correcting an account should displace the court's weighing of the testimony entirely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A would accept passage B's description of oral histories as structured discourse whose authority depends on ceremonial setting.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage B would reject as unnecessary passage A's proposal to assess continuity of transmission and cross-line consistency.

explanations.correct: Passage A's remedy addresses the weighting step; passage B's concern is that even before weighting, the testimony is converted into affidavits and individual factual assertions stripped of ceremonial context. So passage B would regard A's remedy as improvement but insufficient for 'genuine reception,' which requires admitting the community's verifying procedures into the court's weighing.
explanations.A: Directly contradicted; passage B locates the shortfall upstream of A's remedy.
explanations.C: Passage B proposes that community procedures 'enter into' the court's weighing, not displace it entirely.
explanations.D: Passage A does not endorse B's specific claim about ceremonial setting; it may be neutral, not affirmative.
explanations.E: Passage B says genuine reception 'would involve' admitting community procedures — a step beyond A's criteria, not a replacement that rejects them as unnecessary.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following features of oral histories is emphasized in passage B but does not appear in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The continuity of a history's transmission across generations

choices.label: B
choices.text: The consistency of a history's content across independent lines of transmission

choices.label: C
choices.text: The community's procedures for verifying a history's content

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ceremonial setting in which a history is told and the entitlement of its teller

choices.label: E
choices.text: The susceptibility of a history to ordinary cross-examination

explanations.correct: Passage B uniquely describes oral histories as embedded in a setting where 'the ceremonial setting in which it is told' and 'who is entitled to tell it' are constitutive of the history's authority. Passage A mentions none of this.
explanations.A: Passage A explicitly cites 'the continuity of its transmission.'
explanations.B: Passage A cites 'the consistency of its content across independent lines of transmission.'
explanations.C: Passage A cites 'the community's procedures for verifying it.'
explanations.E: Both passages discuss cross-examination, not unique to B.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following judicial practices would, according to passage A, most clearly exemplify the uneven implementation the passage criticizes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court admits an oral history into evidence and, finding that a colonial official's written report contradicts it, treats the report as controlling because written records are easier to verify.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court admits an oral history into evidence and, finding that it is contradicted by three independent written sources whose authors had no connection to one another, gives the written sources greater weight after considering the oral history on its own terms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A court refuses to admit an oral history at all, on the ground that it cannot be tested by documentary cross-reference.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court admits an oral history and corroborates it against a community-administered record of the same tradition before assessing its weight.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court admits both a colonial official's written report and an oral history and concludes that the two sources are not in fact contradictory.

explanations.correct: Passage A specifies the flaw precisely: discounting oral histories against any contradicting documentary source on the ground that written records are more easily verified. (A) matches this description exactly.
explanations.B: This is the evenhanded treatment passage A endorses — weighing the oral source 'on its own terms' before reaching a conclusion.
explanations.C: This is outright exclusion, not the implementation problem passage A describes (which arises after admission).
explanations.D: This describes corroboration against community procedures, the kind of oral-source-appropriate assessment passage A endorses.
explanations.E: No contradiction arises, so no discounting takes place; passage A's criticism does not apply.

questions.questionStem: In passage B, the statement that a court which admits testimony but assesses it by unsuitable criteria "has not, strictly speaking, excluded it" functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: concede the technical accuracy of a characterization the author then qualifies in order to advance a stronger claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: reject as false the claim that admission and genuine reception are distinct achievements

choices.label: C
choices.text: refute passage A's description of uneven implementation in Canadian courts

choices.label: D
choices.text: propose that Canadian courts stop admitting oral histories until a new standard is settled

choices.label: E
choices.text: provide an example of ceremonial testimony processed through the adversarial format

explanations.correct: The author grants that technically the court has admitted the testimony (no formal exclusion), then pivots: 'but it has processed it through a format that converts it into something the testifying community would not recognize.' The concession sets up the stronger claim about format-driven distortion.
explanations.B: The statement in fact sets up that very distinction; it does not reject it.
explanations.C: Passage B does not refute passage A; the two passages are compatible.
explanations.D: Passage B does not propose halting admission.
explanations.E: The clause does not supply an example; it is a concessive move about the court's formal status.
